items.title: Fannie Mae logs title, appraisal savings; net revenues soar
items.description: Fannie Mae Fannie Mae logs title, appraisal savings; net revenues soar By Bonnie Sinnock CloseText About Bonnie twitter bcynic mailto bonnie.sinnock@arizent.com linkedin bonnie-sinnock-115a829 Published October 28, 2026, 5:29 p.m. EDT 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: Why Fannie Mae came out ahead in earnings despite mixed impacts from higher rates, and has new reason to press forward with title alternatives. Supporting Data: Fannie found borrowers' collective savings from appraisal and title alternatives so far this year have been over $100 million. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Fannie Mae reported its highest net revenues since 2023 and revealed significant mission-related borrower savings from title and appraisal alternative initiatives in the third quarter, when it contended with mixed impacts from higher rates but was still able to hold costs for lenders relatively low. Consumer savings from the title and appraisal waiver programs show these alternatives got enough use to drive a 7-figure reduction in origination expenses. They also reinforce a recent executive order backing both and transitioning Fannie's title alternative pilot to a national program with monitoring. Processing Content "Our efforts to provide appraisal and title insurance alternatives helped borrowers save an estimated $141 million in closing costs so far this year," Peter Akwaboah, acting CEO and chief operating officer at Fannie Mae said during the government-related loan buyer's earnings call. Peter Akwaboah, acting CEO and chief operating officer at Fannie Mae Fannie was able to support such housing affordability initiatives with $4.2 billion in net income, representing a 5% rise from the previous quarter and an 8% increase from a year ago, even though higher rates diminished the industry originations it buys. The government-sponsored enterprise's executives explained why during its earnings call. Why fewer acquisitions didn't hurt revenue "Changes in interest rates affect various aspects of our financial results. For example, in single-family, while higher rates tend to reduce acquisition volumes, they also slow prepayments and book runoff, helping to preserve guaranty revenues," Chief Financial Officer Chryssa Halley noted during the company's call. Fannie's core guaranty business fueled 79% of its $7.7 billion in total net revenues, which drove the government-sponsored enterprise's earnings gain. Single-family loan acquisition volumes did fall by roughly 21% from the previous quarter and around 11% from a year earlier to $88 billion in line with some industry declines, but with refinancing representing only $18 billion of that total, prepayments for Fannie were reduced. Refi activity in the dominant single-family business matched year-ago levels but was down nearly 53% from the previous quarter. In addition to affecting prepayments and loan volume in the quarter, this may have another impact, according to Halley. "From an allowance perspective, slow prepayments extend the expected life of our loans, which combined with higher mortgage costs for certain borrowers can increase our expected credit losses," she said. Serious and 60-day delinquencies in the single-family sector remained historically low but have been drifting generally higher in the past year, ending at 62 and 92 basis points, respectively, in the third quarter. They were both nearly 20 basis points lower than a year earlier. Sixty-day delinquencies were 7 basis points lower the previous quarter. Serious delinquencies were 4 basis points lower compared to the same period. Thirty-day delinquencies matched the previous quarter's 1.09%, but were below the 1% level reported a year earlier. Fannie recorded a total single- and multifamily allowance for credit losses of $1.1 billion, offset by other developments that included $630 million in fair value gains. The GSE also reported $94 million in investment gains. It additionally took $1 billion in net unrealized losses in its available-for-sale portfolio. Efficiency initiatives and regulatory capital Fannie also engaged in further efficiency initiatives during the quarter that Halley said offset some personnel costs for increased salaries, benefits and a $28 million severance expense. Expenditures on occupancy and technology were $52 million lower than the previous quarter. Fannie reported a total adjusted capital deficit of $11 billion for the quarter, down from $14 billion in the previous three-month period. Its illustrative return on average required tier 1 capital was 11.1% in the quarter, up from 10.8%. "Despite volatility across aspects of our financial results, we increased net income both quarter over quarter and year over year, growing net worth to more than $119 billion while reducing our regulatory capital deficit," Halley said. items.title: The housing market gets a positive Fed day for a change
items.description: On Wednesday we got an October surprise: the Fed day was eerily calm, with Fed Chair Kevin Warsh looking comfortable on stage and offering a slightly dovish take on the future — if a few things improve. I believe the Fed wants to take back all the interest rate cuts from last year, and then they can assess what is happening in the economy. Of course, the Iran conflict and Trade War 2.0 have complicated their job, but today, given that markets were at one point pricing in five to six rate hikes, was a positive day. Last I checked, the 10-year was at 5.02%, down after Google reported a bad quarter. The Fed's press statement was short and simple, but two things caught my attention. 1. The economy is strong vs. solid First, the Fed chose to use the word "strong" instead of "solid" on purpose to signal it won’t cut rates and will continue reversing last year's interest rate cuts while inflation stays above target. “ Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.” Warsh said jobless claims data remain low and that the Fed fully intends to bring inflation back to the 2% target, no compromise. He also said the Fed will hold one fewer voting meeting in 2027 and two fewer meetings in 2028; this approach might leave the Fed open to more 50-basis-point cuts or hikes. However, that is another story for another time. 2. Warsh liked the market drama against AI I got a strong sense that Warsh liked the market getting more restrictive and that we even saw some AI companies shed some blood recently. My theme in the HousingWire Daily podcast lately borrows from The Predator movie: the AI god king can bleed — and that it means you can kill it. I think Warsh was implying no company is invincible, and that if the market gets more restrictive, things can change, as they recently did. He also talked about how the 10-year yield rolled over even though oil prices have been elevated this month. I believe the 10-year yield rollover is more market-driven, as the 10-year was pricing in more rate hikes than the Fed was targeting at the time. The term premium on the 10-year yield was elevated as it headed to the October high. If the 10-year had closed over the key level of 5.35%, bond yields had the potential to rise much higher, faster, as the markets would be pricing in a much more aggressive Fed rate hike cycle, but, smartly, they chose not to go that route. Warsh seems to enjoy that everyone is taking the Fed seriously and that the markets have already done a lot of the work for them. This reaffirms my assumption that all they want to do is take back the rate cuts from last year and then reassess what is going on. One side note was that Fed Governor Lisa Cook — who is usually a dove — voted to raise rates, which I 100% believe was a trolling tactic on her part since Trump still wants to fire her . All in all, it wasn’t a bad day; the 10-year yield is above 5% still today, but considering the market was trying to price in five to six rate hikes, and there hasn’t been any end to the conflict or the trade war, I consider this a victory for the month of October. For housing, the worst-case scenario has been averted and we bought some time, giving space for the conflict to end and the trade war to cool off a bit. What I am hoping for is that we get some more clarity on both of those two items, and then the Fed can make the rate hike cycle just a few rate hikes, and then we'll take it from there. Related More: Federal Reserve

items.title: Alexander brothers sentenced to 30 years for sex trafficking
items.description: Luxury real estate brokers Oren and Tal Alexander along with their brother Alon, each got sentenced to 30 years in federal prison for sex trafficking. This sentencing comes after the brothers were convicted in March of 2026. The judge called the brothers’ conduct “monstrous” in their sentencing, according to a report by The Associated Press . Over the course of their trial, 11 women testified, describing being raped or sexually assaulted after they became disoriented after being given a drink by one of the brothers. Attorneys for the brothers said they had apologized to the women they insulted or offended for conduct they admit was “insensitive toward the feelings of certain women at certain times,” however they added that the brothers “steadfastly maintain their complete innocence of these awful charges.” Rape allegations against the brothers began emerging in 2024, resulting in Tal and Oren Alexander stepping away from their firm Official Partners in June 2024. Legal challenges against the brothers began piling up in the second half of 2024, eventually leading to their arrests in December 2024. Through out 2025 they faced mounting civil and criminal lawsuits, leading to them eventually being found guilty of sex trafficking in March of 2026. Related More: Alexander brothers

items.title: Bisnow's 2026 New York Power Women
items.description: There were plenty of reasons for New York City’s commercial real estate titans to turn pessimistic in 2026 — if that were in their nature. Courtesy of Montephoteaux Awards from Bisnow's 2025 Power Women Ceremony Persistent inflation has kept interest rates elevated, the 10-year Treasury yield surpassed 5% and stayed there, and institutional equity has stuck to the sidelines. On a local level, the industry is navigating a new left-wing mayoral administration — one that has promised to toughen its approach to landlords — and watching a coming gubernatorial election. But the last thing true New Yorkers would do is bet against New York. That’s why, despite the changing landscape and increasing pressures, this year has been defined by new record office rents , skyline-shaping groundbreakings and potential solutions for the housing crisis. Every year, Bisnow honors a group of women for their excellence in leadership, innovation, influence and impact on the business capital of the world. Each plays a key role in moving the market forward. Women represent 26% of C-suite executives and 33% of board members at large commercial real estate companies, according to a Bisnow analysis of the industry. Despite being a minority, this year’s honorees are powerful dealmakers, indispensable leaders and supportive mentors. Many are also caring mothers, giving philanthropists and cherished friends. These women were nominated by peers in their respective fields across development, asset management, brokerage, capital markets, policy and more. A steering committee evaluates the nominations and selects the honorees. This year’s steering committee consisted of RXR’s Whitney Arcaro, BGO’s Abbe Franchot Borok, Scotiabank’s Linda Foggie, Hunton Andrews Kurth’s Laurie Grasso and Harbor Group International’s Lesley Lisser. Join Bisnow in celebrating the honorees at the New York Power Women Cocktail & Award Ceremony on Nov. 4 at 5:30 p.m. The event will be held at Silverstein Properties ’ 3 World Trade Center. Get tickets here . items.title: Microsoft, Coca-Cola, Amazon Adapting Offices For AI Age
items.description: The use of artificial intelligence is driving the world's largest companies to reassess their workforce — and workspace — in the pursuit of efficiency. The technology is reshaping how employees work and collaborate, prompting employers to reevaluate their office layouts to promote more integrated workspaces, workplace and real estate executives for Microsoft , Citadel , Amazon and Coca-Cola Co. said during a panel at the Urban Land Institute 's fall meeting Tuesday in Miami Beach. Bisnow/Chloe Gallivan Citadel Chief Workplace Officer Paul Darrah speaks at ULI's fall 2026 conference in Miami Beach. Not only are companies starting to use AI to design their spaces, but they are also reconfiguring their spaces away from isolated workstations and toward a more open and collaborative environment, the executives said. "I think AI is going to have a big impact on corporate, like our spaces that we use," said Terri Lasoff, senior director of global real estate portfolio for Coca-Cola, which is using AI for internal data, generating ads and throughout the creative process. "When we think about our spaces at work — and I know we've moved there with hybrid work where you have less 'me spaces,' more 'we spaces' — but does AI continue to drive that where the reason you're coming into the office isn't to do the heads-down, build the deck, do the report?" she added. AI has already created a fundamental difference in the office market, as companies focused on the technology are leasing office space at rapid rates , making them among the most active sectors in the market. But the technology's growing adoption is also expected to keep office-using job growth flat and has led to mass cuts to company headcounts, fueling growing concerns that automation is taking over the workforce. In a global survey of more than 6,000 employees and business leaders, 40% said they expect AI to help employees be more productive, while 28% expect it to reduce headcount, according to an October Workday report . Microsoft announced earlier this week that it was offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, more than a quarter of its global workforce, in addition to the 4,800 employees the company announced it would lay off in July, Reuters reported . When the news broke Monday, Microsoft's head of global workplace services, Elizabeth Schryer, was on a plane to Miami for the conference. She said onstage it made her think about what it meant for the workspace. "I would really say that it points to the biggest thing, which is workforce shifts not just in size but also in location and the move to bring people together in the office experience and collaboration," Schryer said. "AI in general is huge for everybody," she added. "It's huge for all of us ... including companies who are deep in the middle of it [and] are trying to figure out what it means to us and our teams and our businesses, the domain in which we work, and how to use it." Microsoft, which expects to spend roughly $175B on AI infrastructure in 2026, is developing new AI models and using it internally in many ways. The workplace strategy team is starting to use AI to design and create renderings of proposed workspaces like offices, campuses and event areas, reducing time and cost, Schryer said. Bisnow/Chloe Gallivan Hines' Whitney Burns, Citadel's Paul Darrah, Microsoft's Elizabeth Schryer, Amazon's Sean Lee and Coca-Cola's Terri Lasoff at ULI's fall 2026 conference in Miami Beach Amazon, among the most aggressive companies in its push to use AI to reduce its payroll, announced last year that it would cut 14,000 corporate positions and plans to cut as many as 30,000 more as AI pushes quicker innovation. Sean Lee, the company's global real estate and facilities leader, said his team's AI usage jumped from roughly 7% in January to more than 90% this month, allowing team members to spend more face time with clients rather than at their desks. "We're extremely lean as a team, so bandwidth is constrained," Lee said. "What we found is AI, as a supplement to work, is creating bandwidth so that people are doing higher-level thinking at this point. "They can knock out papers faster, they can put presentations together, they can do all of that stuff really easily, which is then giving them the time to take a step back and look at what's going on with my customer." Citadel hasn't made any moves to cut jobs because of AI. On the contrary, it is building its own headquarters tower in Miami and another in New York , two of the biggest office projects in the country. The hedge fund's billionaire founder and CEO, Ken Griffin , owns the combined 3.5M SF office towers underway, but he has shared concerns over the danger AI poses to white-collar jobs. Still, the firm is leveraging AI internally to "further accelerate their research process," Griffin said at a New York conference last December, Business Insider reported . Citadel is focused on employee synergy, Chief Workplace Officer Paul Darrah said, and is often reconfiguring spaces to improve upon it, especially as internal teams realign and move around. That includes taking the reins on moving a landlord's staircases or taking over the fire exits when they lease space in an office building to boost efficiency and interconnectivity, he said. "I'm going to say our competitive advantage is our in-office culture," Darrah said. "We bring employees together to collaborate. We build community, and so for us, being in the office is paramount. "How we think about delivering our workplace, to ensure high performance of our teams but also elevate the experience of the employee — both of those things are really important." items.title: Standard Communities Begins Investing In Philadelphia
items.description: Standard Communities sees promise in greater Philadelphia’s attainable and affordable housing space. The firm announced Wednesday it has closed a $29.3M acquisition of the 186-unit Helston Apartments at 3801 Conshohocken Ave. in Wynnefield Heights. This is the firm’s first property in the area, and it said it has earmarked another $150M for purchases in the region. Courtesy of Standard Communities The Helston Apartments at 3801 Conshohocken Ave. “We’re here for the long term,” Standard Senior Managing Director of Essential Housing Christopher Cruz said in a statement. “This investment is a great example of how private capital can be used to preserve affordability for Philadelphia’s workforce,” he added. The mid-rise apartment complex built in 1970 will receive $4M in renovations, in part to address deferred maintenance. More than half of its current residents make less than 80% of the area median income. Standard holds $7B of assets, including about 30,000 housing units across 22 states and Washington, D.C. SALES Hatfield-based Clemens Development has purchased the Mill Town Square shopping center in Downingtown from Tripoint Properties for $22.4M, the Philadelphia Business Journal reported . The property, which spans 8.7 acres at 150 E. Pennsylvania Ave., is anchored by Planet Fitness. *** Pearl Properties has spent $3M on three lots adjacent to 708 Sansom St. on Jeweler’s Row, where the developer is entitled to build a 34-story residential tower, the PBJ reported . CONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT Greystar has broken ground on a 150-acre South Jersey industrial project at 744 Creek Road in Bellmawr. The firm expects to deliver a 406K SF building and a 249K SF building by January 2028. CBRE will manage the lease-up. *** Courtesy of Buccini Pollin Group The Standard in downtown Wilmington Buccini Pollin Group has completed the 100-unit third phase of the Standard at Market West in Wilmington. The new units at 221 W. 10th St. are already 50% leased, and the multifamily component of the project is 90% occupied overall. FINANCING Regions Real Estate Capital Markets has arranged an $81M series of loans for an undisclosed Philadelphia multifamily player from ACORE Capital. It includes a $36M construction loan for 120 units at 1330 N. American St. in Olde Kensington, $28M in bridge financing for 70 units at Germantown Row, and $17M for 44 units at Binder Terrace Apartments in Ludlow. The deal was led by a Regions team including Jason Hull, Rickey Mirabito and Sean Reilly. PEOPLE Investment firm Matthews has hired Philadelphia-based Michael Inforzato as a first vice president in its senior housing division. He previously spent six years in the same sector at Marcus & Millichap, which followed more than a decade in healthcare operations. *** Trophy Commercial Real Estate has added Sajan Shah to its team as a vice president. The Temple University graduate has a track record of $75M in gross sales. THIS AND THAT Ensemble Investment and Orchestra Life Sciences have teamed up to launch a workforce training program called KAAZI at 1200 Intrepid Ave. in the Philadelphia Navy Yard. The program, with a focus on advanced manufacturing, will train cohorts of 12 to 16 people for three months. items.title: Philly Hospitals Seek Cost Savings From Architects, Builders
items.description: Hospitals across greater Philadelphia face a challenging operating environment, and with federal support expected to dry up, executives are looking to the ancillary businesses they work with for help. Pexels/K Architecture and construction firms that depend on these projects can do more to help keep capital budgets in check as healthcare systems respond to sustained patient demand, CEOs from across the region said Tuesday at Bisnow ’s Pennsylvania Healthcare Real Estate Summit, held at the Crystal Tea Room in Philadelphia. “You’ve got to help us in our ecosystem,” University of Pennsylvania Health System CEO Kevin Mahoney said. “Get on our team. We’re getting paid less.” The Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia is spending nearly $2.6B to build a new patient tower in West Philadelphia, CEO Joseph Mitchell said. The 20-story building is due in 2028. While he is proud of the project, Mitchell said the institution can’t afford to keep spending like this in the current climate. “That’s just unaffordable in the long term,” he said. “Partner with your clients to find ways to reduce these costs. It’s a two-way street.” Hospitals' already strained operating margins are facing more issues from federal spending cuts that lead to an increase in uncompensated care. Last year's One Big Beautiful Bill Act included a $1T cut to Medicaid through 2034, which is expected to cause more than 10 million Americans to lose their health insurance coverage over that period. This is a particularly grave issue for cash-strapped rural hospitals. More than 100 have shuttered over the past decade, and another 700 are at risk of closing, according to a July report from the Center for Healthcare Quality and Payment Reform. Hospitals face additional economic challenges when looking to build new facilities. Construction costs across Eastern Pennsylvania were up 2.2% month-over-month and 11.2% year-over-year in September, according to a report from the local branch of Associated Builders and Contractors. Mitchell acknowledged that construction costs are ballooning across the U.S. and that health systems sometimes don’t pick the cheapest ways to do projects. For example, CHOP has opted to utilize union labor on the tower. Last-minute changes to hospital projects that are commonplace in the industry also add extra costs, Mitchell said. But ultimately, the executive said something has to break: “Can we find ways to limit astronomical growth in capital spending?” Bisnow/Noah Zucker LF Driscoll's Mike Dikon, Thomas Jefferson University's Joseph Cacchione, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia's Joseph Mitchell, Tower Health's Michael Stern, Highmark Health's Karen Hanlon, Geisinger's Terry Gilliland, Cooper University Health Care's Anthony Mazzarelli and University of Pennsylvania Health System's Kevin Mahoney Mahoney suggested that less traditional construction techniques could be part of the solution. He said Penn Medicine’s 17-story, 504-bed Pavilion came online in West Philly in 2021 after the system spent $1.6B. The project was 30% modular, Mahoney said. He thought projects should be closer to 70% prefabricated as a way to rein in construction budgets. Penn Medicine signed a 40K SF lease for its first Delaware location in February. The space in suburban Wilmington will be focused on primary care and some specialty services. Artificial intelligence is just as hot a topic in the design and building world as anywhere else, but Cooper University Health Care CEO Anthony Mazzarelli said healthcare systems aren't seeing the technology create shorter construction timelines or anything else that would save them money. “That's how long that took two years ago. You just told me you're using all this AI stuff. How are you passing on that efficiency to us?” he said. “We're the one throat to choke from the government when it comes to spending, but it's also going to hurt everybody else.” Earlier at Tuesday's event, a different panel was asked about unconventional techniques that could be used to expedite projects. CHOP Assistant Vice President of Facilities Project Management and Construction Brian Gardner floated organizationwide standardized construction plans. While designing and coming to a consensus on those plans can be an arduous process, he said the work pays off down the line and is one of the few meaningful levers healthcare systems can pull to shorten construction timelines. "Standardization is probably one of the low-hanging fruits that organizations can work through because decisions come quicker,” Gardner said. The CEOs’ pleas for cost savings come as regional hospital system players expect higher construction prices in Pennsylvania amid the data center boom. Many of the contractors and suppliers that hospital systems depend on have been focused on getting a piece of the artificial intelligence data center boom, a trend that is already making it harder to build healthcare projects in other markets, like Houston . “We’re already seeing it with the data centers, believe it or not,” Guthrie Senior Vice President Joseph Sawyer said. He recalled being given a yearlong lead time for critical components such as generators and air handlers. Increased competition for construction workers is also straining construction budgets. “How do we address, when we’re trying to do pro formas nationally, the impact of 50% labor increases because we can’t find enough qualified labor?” Limbach Vice President Jay Levin said. KQT Health owner Todd Strine said he believes there is no end in sight and that it would behoove health systems to expedite their construction decision-making. “Prices are going to go way up,” he said. “If you’re going to make a large decision, I think it’s better to do it sooner than later.” See more photos from Tuesday's event below.
